title: Experts Discuss Hypersonic Travel’s Impact on Medical Transport

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: No, no, it's all good. Thank you, man, I appreciate it. Great. You talked about, uh, organ transplants briefly. Uh, can you explain a little bit more about like the timelines that are permissible for organ transplants and what it would mean to, um, to the medical industry to have a plane like this?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: If you think about the organ transplant, if you're in a donor list and a donor appears, they have only 30 to 40 minutes to to start preparing the operation. So you need to be 30, 40 minutes away from the hospital to be included in that list. So if it takes you 2 hours to be anywhere in the world, now 1 hour will put you almost half away in the world. So basically your chances of getting a donor of the transplant list increases because you can be close to more hospitals. Amazing.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Are there any other examples you can think of, of things like that, that the average person would not connect that this is going to change?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: This basically changes everything. If you think, yeah, so thinking about how the distance shrink, that starts to change everything. Let's say you need to do a treatment that is once a month and you go to your local hospital. Now you can do that half around the world. So does it make sense to have high-complexity hospitals when you can get any patient anywhere in the world in under 2 hours? Maybe now is the time to have a hub where we have all the complexity, we take care all of that, and people just get transport in.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: In the same way that emergency response people now might, you know, use a helicopter to take you to a hospital or something, do you picture there being medical-specific use cases here where a city would have one of your planes ready to go at all times for emergency medical treatment? Or maybe like a place that— yeah, I mean, are you expecting there to be adoption of these by companies who have these like tight turnaround timelines?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: One of the things is when you think about airplanes that do transport for patients, they usually can fly 2, 3 hours, maybe, from one small city to one big city. Now with this aircraft, if you do the same process, you can get anywhere in the world. So an emergency in a small town in Africa can now be treated in New York, can be treated in Dallas. So if you have a critical patient that's going to be air transport, you don't have to go to your designated hospital. You can go anywhere in the world that have an availability for for you. So now people get an accident in New York and can be treated in Dallas or can be treated in even Europe.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: How long will it take to get from Los Angeles to New York?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: So one of the things about thinking big travel, it's also small travel. This aircraft will not make sense for short distances. But something like New York to Los Angeles, it will take about an hour, an hour and a half. And that's kind of the minimum distance that this aircraft makes sense.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Can I ask the question? Yeah. Like, if this, like, aircraft is so fast, how is it going to impact the people in it? Like, people, jet fighters, like pilots of the jet fighter?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: One of the most common questions about this aircraft is what happens with people? They're going to get pushed back into the seats. They're going to die. They're going to feel like a rocket. And the answer is no. We're going to have a very smooth takeoff and landing process, the same way that you do with the current aircraft. And then we're going to have a small acceleration sustained for a few minutes. So getting to Mach 10 will take 20-30 minutes, so you don't feel the acceleration. That's why this aircraft will be flying at least for an hour, an hour and 20. So it doesn't make sense for short flights. You have more?

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: No. Feel free if you do. Um, what will the experience— how will the experience be different for people than what they're used to now?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: Mostly the experience flying on the aircraft will be the same as today because the aircraft will be the interiors designed by the airlines like they do with any airplane today. Think about those small regional airplanes that fly LA to San Francisco, which is 2 rows of seats, very small. And that's kind of the size inside the airplane. Uh, the feeling when flying will be very similar to flying any airplane, and the kind of services and the comfort of the chairs will be an airline decision.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Are there things you're already doing, even in this early stage, to connect with governments or to start talking to LAX about having this work there? Like, what are you doing now in in the early stages to make sure that like this is an acceptable thing for the bureaucracies and companies and airports when you're ready to go?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: One of the main advice from YC is launch soon. We unfortunately cannot launch soon, but we can do is talk to customers and we are doing that. We are constantly having conversations with the United States Air Force. We are talking with the Space Force. We are talking with 2 airlines that I cannot mention. And ideally, we do this to start discussing with them how our design is looking like. Hey, do you think this is the range? Do you think this is the speed? Do you think this is the flexibility that you need?

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: You—

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: we have in conversations with the Space Force and with the United States Air Force that they have been working on hypersonics for decades. So they are helping us validate our ideas. They are helping us validate our approach. We've been in conversations with NASA, and NASA is helping us design our Telma protection systems. They're telling us, yes, we saw this work, we think this will not work. So ideally, that helps us de-risk what we are building. And the moment we go to market, there's something that we have been bringing along with our partners. Another important thing for us is to talk to the customers of our customers. So when I talk to a business traveler, I ask, would you be willing to pay what you pay for business to fly an economy seat, but instead of 16 hours flying 2? So that gives us an idea of, okay, these people are willing to pay the cost, they're willing to do the transition when the time comes.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: What is it going to cost to take a flight and how will that pricing change over time?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: In terms of pricing, we are trying to structure it in a way that distance wise will be the same as a business class seat. And the way to think about that is hypersonics use a lot more fuel but also are a lot more faster, so that kind of keep the amount of fuel per distance manageable. Also, we are planning to remove business class seat and put economy class seat. That kind of puts a lot more people into the cabin, which also help us keep the cost low. And if you think in terms of operations, rather than having two crews, having them there, having to fly them back, it's just out and back, simplifying operations for airlines. So all in all, we think the cost will be around of a business class ticket initially. And as we move forward and we keep iterating, we should get to the point where you can fly hypersonic for the cost of economy today.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: What might not— what's something that, uh, might affect the price that you're able to offer, which at this moment still isn't clear?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: One of the biggest open questions here is government regulation, tax, uh, environmental fees. We are not certain about how the government would think about those, and also that has a big impact in terms of what we can offer. And the biggest technical unknown in terms of pricing for us is fuel consumption. We have been doing math and models and we are getting better and better, but until we don't start flying, we will not know exactly the operational cost of the aircraft.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: If somebody were to see this video in the next month, which means in mid-2026, When is the first time they're going to be able to go and buy a ticket and get on one of these planes and fly somewhere around the world in 2 hours?

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: 4 years from now. From— for them, not for us, for them. So 2030, they should be able to start booking tickets.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Say it one more time in a packaged soundbite.

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: We think customers will be able to start booking tickets 2030? No.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Maybe something like, we think the average person will be able to buy a Stratos flight in 4 years.

transcript.speaker: the
transcript.text: We think that the average person will be able to start buying tickets to fly on Stratos Industries aircraft in about 5 years. Boom. That's a wrap.

transcript.speaker: going
transcript.text: Amazing, dude. Thank you very much.
